title: Surveying
intro: Concise Notes for Competitive Exams — Extended Edition (lectures + online material, diagrams, MCQs & links)
Master handbook covering: Surveying + Exam Practice Pack
Overlapping topics have been merged into one chapter and repeated points removed. Practice MCQs for all parts are near the end; the answer key is the last chapter.

b: Surveying: art of determining relative positions of points on, above or below the earth's surface by measuring distances, directions and elevations.
Two basic principles: (1) work from whole to part (prevents accumulation of errors); (2) locate a new point by at least two independent measurements from known points.
Plane surveying: earth treated as flat; curvature ignored; areas < 250 km² (or ~195.5 km² per some texts).
Geodetic surveying: curvature considered; large areas; done by Survey of Pakistan / national agencies.
Difference between arc and chord over 18.5 km ≈ 1 cm; sum of angles of a spherical triangle exceeds 180° by 1″ per ~196 km² (spherical excess).
By instrument: chain, compass, plane table, theodolite, tacheometric, EDM/total station, GPS, photogrammetric.
By purpose: engineering, military, mine, geological, archaeological.
By object/nature of field: land (topographic, cadastral, city), marine/hydrographic, astronomical.
Cadastral survey: fixes property boundaries. Topographic survey: natural and man-made features with relief.
Representative Fraction (RF) = map distance ÷ ground distance (same units).
Plain scale: two dimensions (e.g. m and dm). Diagonal scale: three dimensions (m, dm, cm).
Vernier: reads finer than smallest division. Least count = 1 MSD – 1 VSD = s/n (s = value of 1 MSD, n = no. of vernier divisions).
Direct (forward) vernier: n VSD = (n–1) MSD. Retrograde vernier: n VSD = (n+1) MSD.
Shrunk scale = shrinkage factor × original scale. Shrinkage factor = shrunk length ÷ original length.
Large scale: 1 cm = 10 m or less (building sites). Small scale: 1 cm = 50 m or more (topographic maps).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Survey of Pakistan: National mapping agency (HQ Rawalpindi) — topographic sheets (1:50,000 standard), geodetic control; heights are referred to mean sea level (Karachi tide gauge).
Scale conversions: 1 cm = 10 m → RF 1:1000; 1 inch = 1 mile → RF 1:63,360.
Diagonal scale: Reads three units (e.g., m, dm, cm) — based on similar triangles.
Principle 1: work from whole to part (prevents accumulation of errors). Principle 2: locate a point by at least two independent measurements.
Systematic (cumulative) errors: same sign and magnitude under same conditions; can be computed and corrected; vary directly with L.
Accidental (compensating) errors: random; follow probability laws; vary with √L.
Positive error: measured length > true length (e.g. tape too short). Negative error: tape too long.
Most probable value: arithmetic mean of equal-weight observations; weighted mean otherwise.
Weight ∝ 1/(variance); weight ∝ number of observations; for levelling weight ∝ 1/distance.
Probable error of mean = probable error of single observation ÷ √n. Standard error ≈ 1.4826 × probable error (PE = 0.6745σ).
Precision: closeness of repeated measurements. Accuracy: closeness to true value.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Accuracy vs precision: Accuracy = closeness to the true value; precision = closeness of repeated observations to each other.
Systematic (cumulative) errors ∝ number of observations (or length); accidental errors ∝ √n.
Suitable for small, open, fairly level areas with simple details. Basis: triangulation (network of triangles).
Well-conditioned triangle: no angle < 30° or > 120°; ideal equilateral (60°).
10 square Gunter chains = 1 acre; 80 Gunter chains = 1 mile.
Tallies at every 5 m (metric chain); brass handles at ends; length measured outside handles.
Invar tape (36% Ni + steel): lowest thermal coefficient (~0.0000009/°C); used for base lines.
Accessories: arrows (10 nos), ranging rods (2 or 3 m, painted 20 cm bands red/white), offset rods, pegs, plumb bob.
Main station, subsidiary (tie) station, base line (longest line), check line (proof line), tie line.
Offset: lateral measurement from chain line to detail. Perpendicular or oblique.
Instruments for right angles: cross staff (open, French, adjustable), optical square, prism square.
Ranging: direct (ends intervisible) and indirect/reciprocal (ends not intervisible due to high ground).
Ch = h²/(2L) (approx) or L(1 – cos θ)
True length = measured length × (L′/L), where L′ = incorrect tape length, L = nominal length.
True area = measured area × (L′/L)².  True volume = measured volume × (L′/L)³.
Chaining obstacles: (a) chaining free, vision obstructed (hill); (b) vision free, chaining obstructed (river, pond); (c) both obstructed (building).
Field book: single-line or double-line; recorded from bottom to top.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Given: A 30 m tape is 5 cm too long; measured length 600 m.
Area: Measured 2 ha with same tape → true area = 2 × (30.05/30)² = 2.0067 ha.
Normal tension: Tension at which sag correction = pull correction: Pn = 0.204 W √(AE)/√(Pn − P₀).
Sag correction is always NEGATIVE; slope correction always NEGATIVE; temperature and pull corrections may be + or −.
Bearing: horizontal angle of a line with a reference meridian.
Whole Circle Bearing (WCB): 0°–360° clockwise from north. Used in prismatic compass.
Quadrantal / Reduced Bearing (QB/RB): 0°–90° from N or S towards E or W. Used in surveyor's compass.
Back bearing = Fore bearing ± 180° (WCB). In QB: same value, change N↔S and E↔W.
WCB, 0° at S end, inverted figures
QB, 0° at N & S, E–W interchanged
Graduated ring fixed to needle (rotates with needle)
Included angle = difference of bearings of the two lines (computed from bearings).
Magnetic declination: angle between true and magnetic meridians. True bearing = Magnetic bearing + declination (E) / – declination (W).
Isogonic lines: equal declination. Agonic line: zero declination. Isoclinic lines: equal dip. Aclinic line: zero dip (magnetic equator).
Declination variations: secular (largest, ~250-year cycle), annual, diurnal (daily, more in summer), irregular (magnetic storms).
Dip: angle of needle with horizontal; 0° at magnetic equator, 90° at magnetic poles. Balanced by rider on needle.
Local attraction: deviation due to nearby iron, rails, cables. Detected when FB – BB ≠ 180°. Correct by starting from a station free of attraction (where difference is exactly 180°).
Closing error in compass traverse adjusted by Bowditch rule (graphically).
Needle: magnetized, broad, flat, on agate cap / jewel pivot. Magnetic poles of earth not fixed.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 4.1 — Whole circle bearing and quadrantal bearing of the same line (WCB 120° = S 60° E).
Rule: A line whose FB and BB differ by exactly 180° is free from local attraction; start corrections from its stations.
Declination: True bearing = magnetic bearing + declination (E) or − declination (W).
Prismatic compass: graduated ring rotates with needle, WCB, readings taken through prism; surveyor’s compass: ring fixed to box, QB, readings taken directly (inverted E–W).
Level surface: parallel to mean spheroidal surface of earth (e.g. still lake).
Datum: reference surface (MSL in Pakistan: Karachi; India: Mumbai).
Reduced Level (RL): height of a point above/below datum.
Bench Mark (BM): fixed point of known RL. Types: GTS (Great Trigonometrical Survey), permanent, arbitrary, temporary.
Line of collimation: line through intersection of cross hairs and optical centre of objective.
Back Sight (BS): first reading after setting up (on known RL point; plus sight). Fore Sight (FS): last reading before shifting (minus sight). Intermediate Sight (IS): between BS and FS.
Change point (turning point): point where both FS and BS are taken.
Height of Instrument (HI) = RL of BM + BS.
Dumpy level: telescope rigidly fixed to vertical spindle; simple and stable.
Tilting level: telescope tilts about horizontal axis with fine screw; main bubble centred each sighting.
Wye (Y) level: telescope removable from Y-supports; easy adjustment but wear.
Automatic (self-levelling) level: compensator; most common now. Digital level: reads bar-code staff.
Levelling staff: self-reading (telescopic/Sopwith, folding) and target staff. Folding staff 4 m; 5 mm graduations.
Temporary adjustments: setting up, levelling up, elimination of parallax (focus eyepiece first, then objective).
Permanent adjustment of dumpy level: two-peg test (axis of bubble tube ⊥ vertical axis; line of collimation ∥ bubble tube axis).
ΣBS – ΣFS = Last RL – First RL
ΣBS – ΣFS = ΣRise – ΣFall = Last RL – First RL
Simple, differential (compound/fly), profile (longitudinal section), cross-sectioning, reciprocal, precise, trigonometric, barometric, hypsometric (boiling point).
Fly levelling: rough levelling to check BM or carry RL to work site.
Check levelling: run at end of day to check the day's work.
Reciprocal levelling: across rivers/valleys; eliminates collimation, curvature and refraction errors. True difference h = [(ha – hb) + (ha′ – hb′)]/2.
Refraction coefficient m ≈ 0.07 (about 1/7 of curvature). Refraction is maximum near ground and at sunrise/sunset.
Equal BS and FS distances eliminate collimation error and curvature-refraction effects.
Sensitivity of bubble tube = angle (in seconds) per one division of tube; α″ = (s/(nD)) × 206265 (s = staff difference, n = divisions moved, D = distance).
Sensitivity increases with radius of curvature of tube, length, larger diameter, low viscosity liquid (spirit/alcohol).
Permissible closing error (K in km): rough 0.100√K, ordinary 0.025√K, accurate 0.012√K, precise 0.006√K m.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 5.1 — Levelling with two set-ups: BS, IS, FS, change point and line of collimation.
Fig. 5.2 — Effect of curvature and refraction on staff readings.
Rise & fall method checks intermediate sights as well: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL. HI method has no check on IS.
Contour: imaginary line joining points of equal elevation.
Contour interval: vertical distance between consecutive contours; constant on a map. Depends on scale, nature of ground, purpose, time & funds.
Horizontal equivalent: horizontal distance between two consecutive contours.
Contour gradient: line on ground maintaining constant inclination (set with Abney level/tangent clinometer/ghat tracer).
Close together = steep slope; widely spaced = gentle slope; uniformly spaced = uniform slope.
Equal spacing straight & parallel = plane surface.
Closed contours with higher values inside = hill; lower values inside = depression (pond).
Two contours never cross except at overhanging cliff; they may merge at vertical cliff.
Contours cross ridge and valley lines at right angles. V-shape with apex towards higher ground = valley; towards lower ground = ridge.
A contour cannot end abruptly; it closes on itself (within or outside map).
Methods: direct (tracing contours on ground; accurate, slow) and indirect (grid of squares, cross sections, tacheometric, spot levels). Interpolation: estimation, arithmetic, graphical.
Uses: intervisibility, catchment area, reservoir capacity, route alignment, earthwork estimation, sections.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 6.1 — Contour shapes for a hill, depression, ridge and valley.
Choice of contour interval: Depends on scale, purpose, nature of ground and time/funds: ≈ 0.5 m flat ground, 1–2 m for buildings/roads, 5–10 m for hilly terrain at small scales.
Interpolation: By estimation, arithmetic calculation or graphical method between spot levels.
A contour cannot split or end inside the map; overhanging cliff is the only case where contours cross; vertical cliff → contours merge.
Field work and plotting done simultaneously; graphical method; suitable for small scale and details; not for wet climate or high accuracy.
Accessories: drawing board, alidade (plain or telescopic), spirit level, trough compass (orientation to magnetic north), U-frame with plumb bob, drawing paper.
Setting up: levelling, centring, orientation. Orientation (most important): by back-sighting (most accurate) or by magnetic needle (compass).
Radiation: from one station; small areas, all points visible.
Intersection (graphic triangulation): two stations; locate inaccessible points; well-conditioned rays.
Traversing: like compass/theodolite traverse; for roads, rivers.
Resection: locate the station occupied by the table from known points.
Two-point problem: two visible known points; needs an auxiliary station; less accurate, more time.
Three-point problem: three visible known points. Solved by: mechanical (tracing paper), graphical (Bessel's method), trial & error (triangle of error / Lehmann's method).

Lehmann's rules: point lies on same side of all three rays; distance from each ray proportional to distance of the station; if station is outside great triangle, point lies outside the triangle of error.
Great circle (danger circle): circle through the three known points; if station lies on it, solution is indeterminate.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Orientation methods: By compass (quick), by back-sighting (most accurate), by resection.
Plane table errors: Non-horizontal board, bad centring, defective alidade, incorrect orientation, drawing errors.
Three-point problem methods: mechanical (tracing paper), graphical (Bessel’s), trial & error (Lehmann’s); two-point problem needs an auxiliary station.
Most precise instrument for horizontal and vertical angles; also used for prolonging lines, levelling, traverse.
Transit theodolite: telescope can revolve 360° about horizontal axis. Non-transit: cannot.
Size: diameter of graduated lower circle (e.g. 10 cm, 12 cm). Least count of vernier theodolite usually 20″.

Levelling head (tribrach with foot screws), lower plate (scale plate) with lower clamp, upper plate (vernier plate) with upper clamp, standards (A-frame), telescope, vertical circle, plate levels, altitude bubble, plumb bob.
Centring: placing vertical axis over station. Transiting (plunging/reversing): turning telescope through 180° in vertical plane.
Swinging: turning telescope in horizontal plane. Right swing = clockwise.
Face left (normal): vertical circle on left of observer. Face right (inverted).
Vertical axis, horizontal (trunnion) axis, line of collimation (line of sight), axis of plate level, axis of altitude level.
Axis of plate level ⊥ vertical axis.
Axis of altitude level ∥ line of collimation (vertical circle index error).
Repetition method: angle measured cumulatively n times on the circle; eliminates graduation errors, improves accuracy beyond least count. Used for single angles.
Reiteration method (direction method): several angles at one station measured successively; closing the horizon; sum should be 360°. Used in triangulation.
Face left + face right mean eliminates: collimation error, trunnion axis error, index error of vertical circle, eccentricity of verniers.
Errors NOT eliminated by face change: plate level error (vertical axis not truly vertical).
Eccentricity of circles eliminated by reading both verniers (A and B).
Deflection angle: angle a line makes with prolongation of previous line (R or L, 0°–180°); used for roads, railways.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Least count of vernier theodolite: Commonly 20″ (vernier) — modern digital theodolites read 1″–5″.
Errors eliminated by face left/face right: Line of collimation not ⊥ horizontal axis, horizontal axis not ⊥ vertical axis, index error of vertical circle, eccentricity of verniers.
Repetition method eliminates errors of graduation and improves accuracy for single angles; reiteration (direction) method for many angles from one station (triangulation).
Traverse: series of connected lines whose lengths and directions are measured.
Closed traverse: forms a closed polygon or starts and ends at known points; check available. Open traverse: no check (roads, rivers, pipelines).
Methods: chain angle, compass (free needle), theodolite (fast needle / included angle / deflection angle), plane table.
Sum of interior angles = (2n – 4) × 90°. Sum of exterior angles = (2n + 4) × 90°. Sum of deflection angles = 360° (algebraic).
Latitude L = l cos θ (N +, S –). Departure D = l sin θ (E +, W –). θ = reduced bearing.
Closing error e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²]. Direction: tan δ = ΣD/ΣL.
Relative precision = e/(perimeter). Typical: compass 1:300–1:600; theodolite 1:1000–1:5000 or better.
Bowditch (compass) rule: correction ∝ length of line. CL = ΣL × (l/Σl). Used when angular and linear measurements are equally precise.
Transit rule: correction ∝ latitude/departure. CL = ΣL × (L/ΣL_arith). Used when angles are more precise than lengths.
Graphical method: compass traverse adjustment by Bowditch principle.
Axis method: when angles are accurate and linear errors are along a particular line.
Consecutive coordinates: L and D of each line. Independent (total) coordinates: referred to a common origin; used for plotting.
Gale's traverse table: tabulation of computations for coordinates.
Omitted measurements: max two unknowns (one length + one bearing, two lengths, two bearings, etc.) can be computed.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 9.1 — Closed traverse: latitudes, departures, closing error and balancing rules.
Relative precision: Closing error / perimeter, e.g., 0.5 m / 2000 m = 1 in 4000.
Bowditch rule when angles and lengths are equally precise; transit rule when angles are more precise than lengths.
Horizontal and vertical distances obtained optically (no chaining); fast; for hilly/broken ground, contouring, route surveys.
Instrument: tacheometer = theodolite with stadia diaphragm (3 horizontal hairs).
Horizontal line of sight: D = (f/i)s + (f + d) = Ks + C.
K = multiplying constant = f/i = 100 (usually). C = additive constant = f + d (≈ 0 with anallactic lens).
Anallactic lens: convex lens between objective and eyepiece in external-focusing telescope; makes C = 0. Internal-focusing telescopes have C ≈ 0 naturally.
Inclined sight, staff vertical: D = Ks cos²θ + C cos θ; V = (Ks sin 2θ)/2 + C sin θ.
RL of staff station = RL of instrument axis ± V – h (h = central hair reading).
Other methods: movable hair (subtense), tangential method (two vertical angles), subtense bar (2 m bar, D = cot(α/2)).
Accuracy of stadia: about 1 in 300 to 1 in 500.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 10.1 — Stadia tacheometry: staff intercept s and horizontal distance D = Ks + C.
Worked example: s = 1.50 m, K = 100, C = 0, horizontal sight → D = 150 m.
Subtense bar: 2 m invar bar; D = (b/2) cot(α/2) — tangential/subtense methods for difficult terrain.
Anallactic lens makes the additive constant C = 0 (multiplying constant K = 100).
Horizontal curves: simple circular, compound (two arcs, same direction), reverse (two arcs, opposite directions), transition (spiral).
Vertical curves: summit (crest) and valley (sag); usually parabolic.

s.t: Simple Circular Curve – Elements (R = radius, Δ = deflection angle)
b: Degree of curve D: angle subtended at centre by a standard chord/arc. For 30 m arc: R = 1719/D; for 20 m arc: R = 1146/D (m). For 100 ft chord: R ≈ 5730/D (ft).
Smaller radius = sharper curve = larger degree.
Linear (chain & tape): offsets from long chord, offsets from tangents (radial/perpendicular), successive bisection of arcs, offsets from chords produced (best linear method).
Offset from chord produced: O1 = C1²/(2R); On = Cn(Cn-1 + Cn)/(2R).
Angular (instrumental): Rankine's method of tangential (deflection) angles — one theodolite + tape; most common. δ (minutes) = 1718.9 C/R.
Two-theodolite method: no tape needed; for rough ground. Tacheometric method also possible.
Purpose: gradual introduction of curvature and super-elevation; radius varies from ∞ (at tangent) to R (at circular curve).
Ideal: clothoid (Euler spiral) — radius × length = constant. Railways: cubic parabola. Highways: lemniscate (Bernoulli) / spiral.
Shift S = L²/(24R).  Spiral angle φ = L/(2R) radians.
Length of transition: by rate of change of centrifugal acceleration L = v³/(CR); by rate of super-elevation; by time rate.
Super-elevation (cant): e = v²/(gR) (theoretical); railways e = GV²/(127R) (G = gauge, V km/h); roads e + f = V²/(127R).
Parabola used: constant rate of change of grade; offsets ∝ square of distance from tangent point.
Length L = (g1 – g2)/r, where r = rate of change of grade.
Sight distance governs summit curve length; headlight distance governs valley curve.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 11.1 — Elements of a simple circular curve: PC, PI, PT, R, Δ, tangent length, long chord, mid-ordinate.
Given: R = 300 m, Δ = 40°, chainage of PI = 1250.00 m.
Tangent length: T = 300 tan 20° = 109.19 m → chainage PC = 1140.81 m.
Curve length: l = π × 300 × 40/180 = 209.44 m → chainage PT = 1350.25 m.
Rankine’s deflection angle: δ (minutes) = 1718.9 c/R for chord length c.
Rankine’s method (theodolite + tape) is most accurate for long curves; offsets from long chord / tangents suit short curves.
From field notes: division into triangles, squares, trapezoids.
Trapezoidal rule: A = (d/2)[O1 + On + 2(O2 + … + On-1)]. Any number of ordinates.
Simpson's 1/3 rule: A = (d/3)[O1 + On + 4(even ordinates) + 2(remaining odd ordinates)]. Needs odd number of ordinates (even number of divisions). More accurate (parabolic boundary).
By coordinates: A = ½|Σ(xi yi+1 – xi+1 yi)|. Also by double meridian distance (DMD) and latitudes/departures.
Planimeter (Amsler polar): A = M(F – I ± 10N + C). M = multiplier, N = zero-mark passings, C = constant (added when anchor inside figure).
Prismoidal (Simpson's) rule: V = (d/3)[A1 + An + 4(even) + 2(odd)]; for single prismoid V = (L/6)(A1 + 4Am + A2). Most accurate.
Prismoidal correction = difference between end-area and prismoidal volumes.
Curvature correction applied when section lies on a curve (Pappus theorem).
Volume from spot levels: borrow pits (grid of squares/triangles). Volume from contours: reservoir capacity.
Mass diagram: cumulative volume vs. chainage; rising = cutting, falling = filling; max ordinate = balance point; used for haul, lead and economical earthwork.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Simpson’s rule condition: Needs an ODD number of ordinates (even number of strips); more accurate than trapezoidal rule.
Planimeter: Area = M (F − I ± 10N + C); zero circle constant C used when anchor is inside.
Prismoidal correction: Volume by prismoidal formula is more accurate; trapezoidal (end-area) formula over-estimates.
Mass-haul diagram: Rising line = cut, falling = fill; balancing line gives free-haul and over-haul for earthwork.
Trapezoidal: A = d[(O₁ + On)/2 + O₂ + … + On₋₁]; Simpson: A = (d/3)[(O₁ + On) + 4Σ even + 2Σ odd].
Network of triangles with one base line measured accurately and all angles measured; other sides computed by sine rule.
Used for large areas, geodetic and control surveys; more economical than traversing in hilly terrain.
Figures: single triangles chain (fast, least check), braced quadrilaterals (best for accuracy), centred polygons, chain of quadrilaterals.
Strength of figure: angles near 60°; avoid < 30°. Braced quadrilateral strongest.
Satellite (eccentric) station: when main station cannot be occupied (e.g. church spire); reduction to centre correction applied.
Intervisibility: height of signal/tower computed using curvature & refraction (h = 0.0673 d²).
Signals: luminous (heliotrope — sun's rays; Gauss), opaque (pole, tripod). Phase error in opaque cylindrical signals.
Base line correction & extension; base net to expand base.
Trilateration: all sides measured (EDM) instead of angles.
Station adjustment, figure adjustment; least squares used for adjustment.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 13.1 — Triangulation figures: chain of triangles, braced quadrilateral and centred polygon.
Satellite station: Used when the true station cannot be occupied; reduction to centre applied to observed angles.
Spherical excess: ≈ 1″ per 196 km² of triangle area — considered in geodetic triangulation.
Trilateration measures all sides (EDM); triangulation measures angles + one base line.
Measures distance by phase difference of modulated electromagnetic waves.
Microwave EDM (tellurometer): long ranges up to 100 km; two instruments.
Visible light (geodimeter, laser): up to 25 km (laser longer).
Accuracy expressed as ±(a mm + b ppm).
Electronic theodolite + EDM + microprocessor + data collector; measures horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance; computes coordinates, RL, area.
Reflectorless total stations use laser; robotic total stations can be operated by one person.
Satellite-based positioning: minimum 4 satellites for 3D position + time (3 for 2D).
GPS (USA, ~31 satellites, 6 orbital planes, ~20,200 km altitude), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China).
Segments: space, control, user. Positioning by trilateration from satellite pseudo-ranges.
DGPS (differential): uses base station correction; sub-metre accuracy. RTK: real-time kinematic; cm-level accuracy.
Errors: ionospheric/tropospheric delay, multipath, clock, orbital, PDOP/GDOP (geometry).
Photogrammetry: measurements from photographs. Terrestrial (ground) and aerial.
Scale of vertical photo S = f/(H – h) (f = focal length, H = flying height above datum, h = ground elevation).
Relief displacement d = r h/H (displacement radial from principal point).
Overlap: forward (longitudinal) ≈ 60%; side (lateral) ≈ 25–30%. Stereoscopic vision requires overlap.
Tilted photo: tilt < 3°. Oblique: high (horizon visible) and low.
Parallax bar: measures heights from stereo pairs. Stereoscope: lens or mirror type.
Remote sensing: data from sensors without contact. Passive (uses sun energy) vs active (RADAR, LiDAR).
GIS: system to capture, store, analyse and display spatial data; raster and vector models.
LiDAR: laser pulses from aircraft/drone to produce DEMs. Drones (UAVs) used for rapid mapping.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
GNSS systems: GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China); RTK-GNSS gives cm-level accuracy using a base station or CORS.
Total station functions: Angle + distance + coordinates; stake-out, resection, area, remote elevation measurement; data downloaded to CAD.
LiDAR & drones: Airborne/UAV laser scanning and photogrammetry produce DEMs/point clouds for roads, dams and mining.
GIS: Stores spatial data in vector (points, lines, polygons) and raster (cells) formats; used in urban planning, irrigation command areas, flood mapping.
EDM types: microwave (long range), infrared/light-wave (most total stations), laser (reflectorless).
Hydrographic survey: water bodies; soundings to find depth; used for navigation, dredging, harbours.
Sounding equipment: sounding rod (shallow), lead line, echo sounder (fathometer; most used).
Locating soundings: cross-rope, range & time intervals, two angles from shore (theodolites), sextant (three-point problem), total station, GPS.
Tide gauges: staff, float (self-registering), weight gauge. Mean sea level from long-term tide records (19-year cycle).
Setting out works: buildings (centre line method), culverts, bridges, tunnels (transfer of alignment underground through shafts).
Mine surveying: weisbach triangle for transferring meridian down a shaft.
Barometric levelling: aneroid barometer; rough heights in hilly regions.
Hypsometry: boiling point of water to find altitude.
Abney level (clinometer): measures slopes, heights; sets out gradients.
Ceylon ghat tracer: sets out gradients in hilly areas.
Indian pattern clinometer, tangent clinometer: vertical angles and gradients.
Box sextant: measures horizontal and vertical angles (up to 120°); hand-held; used in hydrography.
Pantagraph: enlarging or reducing maps. Eidograph: same purpose.
Planimeter: area of plan. Opisometer: length of curved lines on maps.
Optical square: two mirrors at 45°; sets right angles. Prism square: same principle with prism.
Line ranger: locating intermediate point on a line.
Agate cap: used in compass needle pivot.
Prismatic compass: 0° marked at south end of ring (because prism is at opposite side).
In surveyor's compass, E and W are interchanged on the ring.
Sum of interior angles of 6-sided closed traverse = 720°.
Bubble of level tube moves towards the higher end.
Parallax: image not formed in plane of cross hairs; removed by focusing.
HI method preferred for profile and construction work; rise & fall more accurate checks.
Normal tension: pull at which sag and pull corrections cancel.
Sag correction is always negative; slope correction always negative; MSL correction negative for points above MSL.
Error due to bad ranging and bad straightening: cumulative and positive.
Best chain line arrangement: few main lines, well-conditioned triangles, check lines provided.
Contours of different elevations cannot unite to form one contour except at vertical cliff.
Zero dip at magnetic equator; 90° dip at magnetic poles.
Anallactic lens provided in external-focusing tacheometer to make additive constant zero.
Rankine's method: deflection angles; most accurate for setting out long curves.
Simpson's rule needs odd number of ordinates; trapezoidal rule assumes straight boundaries.
Prismoidal formula gives most accurate earthwork volume.
Danger circle in three-point problem: circle through three known points.
Reciprocal levelling eliminates collimation, curvature and refraction errors (not error due to change in refraction between readings).
Combined curvature & refraction correction = 0.0673 d² m (d in km).
Least count of prismatic compass: 30′ (but read to 15′ by estimation). Surveyor's compass: 15′.
